units.title: Unit 47 — Sound
learningObjectives: Describe human voices, accents and degrees of audibility using precise, natural collocations.
Differentiate speech that is loud, harsh, husky, slurred or muffled without confusing these qualities.
Choose idiomatic expressions for thunder, echoes, impacts and different types of silence.

items.example: I could hear a trace of an accent when she spoke in English.
items.note: A trace of indicates a faint sign; with accent it suggests a slight rather than pronounced pronunciation pattern.

items.pt: uma voz muito alta e ressonante
items.example: The announcer welcomed everyone in a booming voice.
items.note: Booming describes a very loud, resonant voice, unlike husky, which concerns its low rough quality.

items.example: The guard gave his instructions in a gruff voice.
items.note: Gruff implies low, harsh or unfriendly-sounding speech; it does not necessarily indicate shouting.

items.example: Do not mutter under your breath if you want everyone to hear your objection.
items.note: Mutter under your breath describes speaking so quietly that others may not understand; under your voice is not idiomatic.

items.example: Her suggestion was greeted with a stony silence from the committee.
items.note: Stony silence conveys deliberate coldness or hostility, not merely an absence of noise.

items.example: You may lose your voice if you keep shouting throughout the concert.
items.note: Lose your voice means become unable to speak normally, often because of illness or vocal strain.

items.example: He was too astonished to utter a word when he heard the result.
items.note: Utter a word is typically used with a negative or restrictive expression such as not, never or too shocked to.

items.pt: um sotaque carregado ou muito marcado
items.example: The actor adopted a broad northern accent for the role.
items.note: Broad describes a strong, easily noticeable regional accent, not a physically wide one.

items.example: The singer has a distinctive husky voice that fans recognise immediately.
items.note: Husky refers to a low, slightly rough voice and can be attractive; gruff is more likely to suggest harshness.

items.pt: enrolar ou arrastar as palavras ao falar
items.example: If you slur your words, listeners may struggle to understand you.
items.note: Slur your words means run speech sounds together so that articulation is unclear, for example through exhaustion.

items.example: We heard muffled voices through the thick wooden door.
items.note: Muffled describes sounds that are blocked or indistinct, rather than words spoken with deliberate hostility.

items.word: make out what is being said
items.pt: conseguir entender o que está sendo dito
items.example: Even with headphones, I could barely make out what was being said in the recording.
items.note: Make out means hear or understand something with difficulty; it is common after can or could in negative contexts.

items.example: Please do not raise your voice during the discussion.
items.note: Raise your voice means speak more loudly, sometimes because of anger; it is different from a naturally booming voice.

items.example: Her colleagues noticed a foreign accent but understood every word.
items.note: Foreign accent identifies pronunciation associated with another language; broad describes the strength of an accent.

items.example: A clap of thunder made everyone jump during the storm.
items.note: Clap is the usual noun for a sudden, loud burst of thunder; cry of thunder is not idiomatic.

items.example: A deathly hush fell over the audience before the verdict was announced.
items.note: Deathly hush suggests an exceptionally deep, unsettling silence, rather than a pleasant quiet atmosphere.

items.example: She shared the good news in a soft whisper so she would not wake the baby.
items.note: Soft modifies whisper naturally, whereas loud whisper creates a contrasting or intentionally paradoxical effect.

items.pt: o silêncio toma conta do ambiente
items.example: Silence descended on the room when the lights suddenly went out.
items.note: Silence descends presents quiet as arriving over a whole place; it often marks an abrupt change in atmosphere.

items.example: A distant echo of the music reached us from the far side of the valley.
items.note: Distant locates the echo far away; nearby echo gives a different spatial impression.

items.example: The incessant noise from the road made it hard to concentrate.
items.note: Incessant suggests something continuous or repeatedly intrusive without relief, unlike intermittent noise.

items.example: The cat moved across the floor and made no sound.
items.note: Make no sound indicates total silence from a person or thing; it is more emphatic than simply being quiet.

items.example: At dawn, silence reigns in the deserted village.
items.note: Silence reigns is a figurative, slightly literary way to say silence dominates a place.

items.example: We heard a dull thud when the heavy box landed on the carpet.
items.note: Dull thud refers to a low, non-ringing impact sound, unlike a sharp crack.

items.example: Sound travels surprisingly far across the lake at night.
items.note: Sound travels refers to sound carrying from one location to another; the phrase often takes an adverb or path.

items.example: She let out a cry when the cold water touched her feet.
items.note: Let out a cry means suddenly make a loud vocal sound; let off a cry is not the usual expression.

items.example: The witness refused to utter a single word until her lawyer arrived.
items.note: A single word strengthens the negative or restrictive reading of utter a word; typically used with refuse or not.

items.example: I heard a faint whisper from the back of the hall.
items.note: Faint emphasises that a voice can barely be heard; it does not describe how close the speaker is.

units.title: Unit 48 — Making things easier
learningObjectives: Compare feasible alternatives and viable options, and select clear approaches to complex tasks.
Break large projects into manageable stages without confusing efficiency with avoiding responsibility.
Describe memory strategies, effort, practice and recall with natural C1–C2 collocations.

items.example: Before moving the furniture, we worked out the easiest way to carry it upstairs.
items.note: Work out means determine a solution through thought, rather than merely perform physical exercise.

items.example: The group explored different ways of reducing electricity use.
items.note: Explore different ways of doing something means consider several approaches before selecting one.

items.example: The committee evaluated three feasible alternatives to the original design.
items.note: Feasible emphasises what can realistically be done, not merely an imaginable possibility.

items.example: Only two viable options remained after the budget was reduced.
items.note: Viable options are choices capable of working successfully in practice; viable often implies practical sustainability.

items.example: We enlisted help from experienced volunteers to organise the event.
items.note: Enlist help means actively recruit people to assist, rather than simply receive advice unexpectedly.

items.example: The teacher adopted a method that made revision less intimidating.
items.note: Adopt a method means decide to use a particular approach regularly or for a specific task.

items.example: A step-by-step approach made the installation easier for beginners.
items.note: Step-by-step describes a planned sequence of manageable stages rather than trying everything at once.

items.pt: dividir uma tarefa em partes menores
items.example: We broke the task down into three stages before assigning responsibilities.
items.note: Break a task down into stages means divide it into smaller parts; down can move after the object.

items.pt: partes administráveis ou fáceis de lidar
items.example: I divided the report into manageable chunks and revised one section each day.
items.note: Manageable chunks are portions small enough to handle effectively; chunks is informal but very common.

items.example: Once you understand the symbols, the procedure is simplicity itself.
items.note: Simplicity itself is an emphatic idiom for something extremely easy to understand or do.

items.example: She refused to take the easy option when a more careful solution was needed.
items.note: Take the easy option may imply choosing what requires less effort, though the easier choice is not always wrong.

items.pt: escolher o caminho mais fácil para fugir da dificuldade
items.example: It would be taking the easy way out to cancel the project without addressing its problems.
items.note: Take the easy way out often disapproves of avoiding responsibility or effort; it is not just choosing an efficient method.

items.example: A trained memory helped the interpreter remember long lists of names.
items.note: A trained memory is one deliberately developed through practice, not necessarily an unusually good natural memory.

items.example: Her ability to remain calm was an immense asset during the negotiations.
items.note: Immense asset means something of exceptionally great value or usefulness, not necessarily a physical possession.

items.example: Students used mnemonic techniques to remember the order of the planets.
items.note: Mnemonic techniques are memory aids, such as letter patterns or associations, for recalling information.

items.example: The new sensor reproduced the measurements with an amazing degree of accuracy.
items.note: Degree of accuracy expresses how precise a result is; amazing functions as an evaluative intensifier.

items.example: She perfected a technique for restoring delicate wooden furniture.
items.note: Perfect a technique means refine it until it works extremely well; perfect here is a verb.

items.example: Our team follows a simple rule: check every measurement twice.
items.note: Simple rule refers to an uncomplicated guideline; a basic principle is a broader underlying idea.

items.example: The trainer explained the safety procedures in a straightforward way.
items.note: Straightforward means easy to follow and without unnecessary complications, not necessarily very short.

items.example: A basic principle of good design is to make controls easy to reach.
items.note: Basic principle names a foundational idea on which a system or method is built.

items.example: A short breathing exercise can help concentrate the mind before an exam.
items.note: Concentrate the mind means focus mental attention; concentrate on something specifies the object of attention.

items.example: The instructions seemed confusing, but the process was perfectly simple.
items.note: Perfectly intensifies simple to mean entirely uncomplicated; it does not mean morally perfect.

items.example: Take the time to read the instructions carefully before you begin.
items.note: Take the time to do something encourages deliberate effort rather than rushing.

items.example: After weeks of practice, she could instantly recall every emergency code.
items.note: Instantly recall means retrieve information from memory immediately, without a prolonged search.

items.example: The presenter divided the lecture into small items of information.
items.note: Items of information treats information as countable pieces because information alone is normally uncountable.

items.example: Despite the difficult terrain, she completed the climb with remarkable ease.
items.note: With remarkable ease means surprisingly easily; this fixed structure includes with and a noun phrase.

items.example: The new editing software had a steep learning curve for our volunteers.
items.note: A steep learning curve conventionally describes a skill that requires considerable early effort to master.

items.example: Learning to maintain your bicycle is worth the effort.
items.note: Worth the effort means the eventual benefit justifies the time and work involved.

items.example: He used a familiar melody to recall information during the test.
items.note: Recall information is the neutral verb-noun pairing for bringing learned facts back to mind.

items.example: We explored the options before deciding where to hold the conference.
items.note: Explore the options is a concise way to express deliberate consideration of available choices.

items.example: You should take the time to learn the keyboard shortcuts.
items.note: The fixed infinitive complement explains what time is invested in; unlike waste time, it presents the effort positively.
